Claude Lévi-Strauss. The French anthropologist who founded structuralism and argued that beneath the surface diversity of cultures lie universal mental structures and logical operations.

Lévi-Strauss developed structuralism, the theory that cultural phenomena — myths, kinship, art — encode underlying logical structures reflecting how the human mind categorizes reality. In 1949, he published The Elementary Structures of Kinship, a monumental analysis of marriage rules and kinship systems across societies. In its pages, he revealed mathematical patterns in how families organize themselves across vastly different cultures.

He conducted fieldwork among the Bororo and Nambikwara peoples of Brazil. His journals from this time became Tristes Tropiques, also known as A World on the Wane, which stands as a canonical ethnographic essay. Later, Lévi-Strauss analyzed myths in The Raw and the Cooked and subsequent volumes, showing how myths transform universal oppositions — nature and culture, raw and cooked, life and death — into locally meaningful narratives.

His work made a profound claim about non-Western peoples. He argued that they are not primitive in thought but employ the same logical operations as Western science. This displaced evolutionism from anthropology, a major shift in how the discipline understood human cognition.

He synthesized insights from linguistics, particularly from Saussure and Jakobson, and from mathematics to argue that human culture is a language-like system. The connections between these domains showed that culture operates through structures as orderly and analyzable as those found in any formal system.
